title: REST, WebSockets & gRPC
summary: How apps talk over the network — REST for resources, WebSockets for live channels, gRPC for fast services.

blocks.markdown:
An **API (Application Programming Interface)** is a defined channel through which one program talks to another — over the network, usually over [http-https](http-https).

- **REST** — request/response over HTTP, text-based, stateless.
- **WebSockets** — persistent two-way channel for real-time data.
- **gRPC** — high-speed binary RPC built on HTTP/2.
- The right choice depends on update frequency, direction, and performance needs.

blocks.subTitle: The three styles at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Quick comparison before diving in.

| Style | Transport | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| REST | HTTP/1.1 | Client asks, server answers |
| WebSocket | TCP (ws://) | Both sides send anytime |
| gRPC | HTTP/2 | Both; streaming supported |

When two services run on different machines, they can't call each other's functions directly — they send **messages over the network**.

- One side acts as a **client** (caller), the other as a **server** (responder).
- The message format, address scheme, and rules for talking are the **API contract**.
- Common transport: [http-https](http-https) on top of [transport-layer](transport-layer) TCP.

blocks.subTitle: Resources and HTTP methods
blocks.markdown:
**REST (Representational State Transfer)** treats every piece of data as a **resource** with a URL.

- Resources are nouns: `/users`, `/orders/42`.
- The action is the HTTP **method**: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove).
- Response is usually **JSON** — a lightweight text format both sides understand.
- Stateless: each request carries everything the server needs; no session memory between calls.

blocks.subTitle: Statelessness
blocks.markdown:
**Stateless** means the server keeps no memory of past requests — each call stands alone.

- The client sends auth (token), params, and context every time.
- Benefit: any server instance can handle any request → easy to scale horizontally.
- Cost: slightly larger requests (headers repeat). Mitigated by HTTP caching.

Endpoints follow a resource-first pattern. Status codes tell the client what happened.

```http
GET    /orders        → 200 OK (list)
POST   /orders        → 201 Created
GET    /orders/42     → 200 OK or 404 Not Found
DELETE /orders/42     → 204 No Content
```

- **2xx** success, **3xx** redirect, **4xx** client error, **5xx** server error.
- Using the right method + code makes the API self-describing.

blocks.subTitle: Polling vs long-polling
blocks.markdown:
REST is request/response — the server can't push unprompted. Two workarounds:

- **Polling** — client asks on a fixed timer (every 5 s). Simple but wastes requests when nothing changed.
- **Long-polling** — client asks; server holds the connection open until new data arrives, then replies. Fewer empty responses but one thread held per client.

blocks.subTitle: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
blocks.markdown:
**SSE (Server-Sent Events)** is a one-way push channel over a single HTTP connection.

- Client opens one GET request and keeps it open.
- Server streams `data: ...` lines whenever it has new data.
- **One-way**: server → client only. Browser reconnects automatically on drop.
- Good for: dashboards, feeds, live scores — anywhere the client just listens.

blocks.subTitle: Full-duplex persistent channel
blocks.markdown:
**WebSocket** upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent, **full-duplex** TCP channel — both sides can send messages at any time without a new request.

- **Full-duplex**: server and client send simultaneously, independently.
- Started with an HTTP **Upgrade handshake**; then the protocol switches to `ws://` or `wss://`.
- Very low overhead per message (no HTTP headers per frame).
- Good for: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing, live trading feeds.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/2 and protobuf
blocks.markdown:
**gRPC** is a remote procedure call framework by Google — call a function on another server as if it were local.

- Runs over **HTTP/2**, which multiplexes many streams on one TCP connection.
- Uses **Protocol Buffers (protobuf)** — a binary, strongly-typed schema. Smaller and faster to parse than JSON.
- You define the API in a `.proto` file; gRPC generates client and server code in any language.
- Supports **streaming**: client stream, server stream, or bidirectional.

blocks.subTitle: Why faster than REST
blocks.markdown:
gRPC outperforms REST in internal service calls for two reasons:

- **Binary encoding** — protobuf payloads are 3-10× smaller than equivalent JSON, less to send and parse.
- **HTTP/2 multiplexing** — many requests share one connection; no head-of-line blocking per request.

Trade-off: harder to debug (not human-readable), and browser support needs a proxy (grpc-web).

| Need | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Public API, CRUD, browser clients | REST |
| Real-time bidirectional (chat, games) | WebSocket |
| High-throughput internal microservices | gRPC |
| Server-push only (feeds, dashboards) | SSE |

- Start with REST — it's universal and tooling is everywhere.
- Add WebSockets only when you truly need server-push or two-way live messaging.
- Use gRPC between backend services where performance is critical.

Common mistakes:

- **Using WebSockets for everything.** Persistent connections are expensive — REST handles most CRUD fine.
- **Ignoring status codes.** Returning 200 for errors breaks clients that rely on them.
- **Polling too fast.** High-frequency polling hammers the server; use SSE or WebSocket instead.
- **Exposing gRPC directly to browsers.** Browsers can't speak HTTP/2 frames raw — use REST or grpc-web at the edge.

blocks.subTitle: What makes an API RESTful?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What makes an API truly RESTful?**

Six constraints from Roy Fielding: **stateless** (no server session), **client-server** (separated), **cacheable**, **uniform interface** (resources + HTTP methods), **layered system**, and optional code-on-demand. In practice: resource URLs, correct HTTP methods, meaningful status codes, and no server-side session.

blocks.subTitle: WebSockets vs REST for live data
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you choose WebSockets over REST?**

When the server needs to push data to the client **without waiting to be asked** — chat, live scores, collaborative editing. REST is request/response only; polling wastes connections. WebSocket gives a persistent full-duplex channel at the cost of connection overhead — worth it when update frequency is high.

blocks.subTitle: Polling vs long-polling vs SSE
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between polling, long-polling, and SSE?**

**Polling** — client asks on a timer; wastes calls when nothing changed. **Long-polling** — client asks; server waits until data is ready, then replies; one thread held open. **SSE** — client opens one HTTP stream; server pushes events as they happen, server → client only. Each is a step up in efficiency.

blocks.subTitle: REST vs gRPC
blocks.markdown:
**Q: REST vs gRPC — when do you pick gRPC?**

For **internal backend-to-backend** calls where throughput and latency matter. protobuf encoding is 3-10× smaller than JSON; HTTP/2 multiplexes calls; and the `.proto` schema enforces a contract. REST wins for public/browser APIs where readability and tooling diversity matter more.

blocks.subTitle: How a WebSocket connection starts
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does a WebSocket connection get established?**

It starts as a normal HTTP GET with an `Upgrade: websocket` header. The server responds with **101 Switching Protocols**. After that, the TCP connection stays open and both sides exchange lightweight **frames** — no HTTP overhead per message. TLS is supported via `wss://`.
